review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: Probiotic supplements are dietary supplements containing live microorganisms intended to confer a health benefit to the host when administered in adequate amounts. These microorganisms, primarily bacteria and yeasts, aim to positively influence the gut microbiome by supporting its balance and diversity. Probiotics function mainly through mechanisms such as competitive inhibition of pathogenic microbes, enhancement of the intestinal barrier, modulation of the immune system, and production of beneficial metabolic compounds. The efficacy of probiotics depends strongly on strain specificity; not all strains exert the same effects, which influences their clinical utility. Probiotics are most commonly used to support digestive health, manage antibiotic-associated diarrhea, and may have emerging roles in immune regulation and mental health through the gut-brain axis. Practical relevance includes guidance on appropriate strain selection, dosing, and storage conditions—many probiotics require refrigeration to maintain viability. Limitations include variability in regulatory standards for supplements, inconsistent quality and labeling, and gaps in evidence, especially for extrapolating benefits beyond gastrointestinal indications. Related concepts include prebiotics, which are nondigestible compounds that foster growth of beneficial microbes, and synbiotics, combinations of probiotics and prebiotics. Understanding these concepts helps consumers make informed decisions regarding probiotic use.
